Chapter 7: The Ethics of Elfland—Wonder and Morality.
You know, there’s a certain kind of wisdom that doesn’t come from textbooks or lectures. It comes from the stories we’re told as kids—the fairy tales with talking animals, enchanted forests, and impossible quests.
Even though the details might fade with time, those stories leave behind lessons that stick with us. They remind us that the world is full of wonder, and that right and wrong aren’t just rules made up by society—they’re deep truths, woven right into the fabric of reality.
Imagine this: a child asks, “Why does the sun rise every morning?” Instead of launching into a scientific explanation, the parent shares a story—maybe about a great king who commands the dawn. Suddenly, the child’s eyes light up. For just a moment, the world feels magical again. And somehow, the rules of right and wrong seem as real and certain as the sun itself.
The old faith—the one built on stories and symbols—really spoke to that sense of wonder. It taught us to see the world not as a cold machine, but as a beautiful work of art. In that world, every action matters. Good and evil aren’t just ideas—they’re real, and the choices we make help shape the story we’re living.
Most of us don’t realize just how much our sense of right and wrong is shaped by the stories we believe. Today, it feels like the modern world wants to turn morality into a checklist or a set of calculations. But the old faith? It saw morality as something much deeper—almost like a response to the beauty and mystery all around us.
Over time, you start to see that living a moral life isn’t just about following rules. It’s about finding your place in the story of creation—seeing yourself as a character in a grand drama. And you’re called to play your part with courage, and with joy.
There’s a real freedom in living this way. Instead of being weighed down by guilt or fear, you’re invited to step into the adventure of goodness. Every act of kindness becomes a small miracle. Every sacrifice is just another step on the journey.
So, what if, at the end of the day, the best way to understand morality is to see our lives as stories—full of wonder, meaning, and the chance to choose what kind of hero we want to be?
